title: The One With The Boob Job

jokes.text: Monica asks 'What?' and Chandler reveals he's been shaving, then corrects himself: 'No, rabies.'
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler rush over in a panic asking what's wrong
jokes.punchline: Chandler casually clarifies the reason for his blood isn't shaving — it's rabies, delivered with complete nonchalance
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler deadpan. The two-step misdirection (shaving → rabies) is tightly constructed and the casual delivery of 'rabies' earns a genuine laugh. Economy is near-perfect: two words do all the work. Character-specific because Chandler's self-deprecating hypochondria is core to his voice.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What's wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Rabies.

jokes.text: Rachel's retort: 'Not so funny when someone does that to you, is it?'
jokes.setup: Ross's fart-on-lap joke implies this is funny/cute when a baby does it
jokes.punchline: Rachel implies Ross has also done this to her, flipping the dynamic and implying he farted on her
jokes.explanation: Quick, economical callback to the previous joke. The implication that Ross has farted on Rachel adds character-based humor. Functional but not exceptional — it's a solid button on joke #2.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can't believe how fast Emma's growing up. I was just thinking about all these precious memories we have together.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That's so sweet, Ross. What's your favorite memory with her?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, there was this one time when she was about three months old, and she farted right in my face.

jokes.text: After a long, completely still silence waiting for Emma to crawl, someone asks 'Who's painting us?'
jokes.setup: Everyone freezes completely still for over a minute waiting for the baby to crawl again — an extended, increasingly uncomfortable silence
jokes.punchline: Joey breaks the silence with the surreal non-sequitur 'Who's painting us?' — the stillness reminded him of posing for a portrait
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The extended silence (nearly 40 seconds of transcript time) makes the absurdist payoff land hard. 'Who's painting us?' is perfectly Joey — not stupid-dumb, but associatively weird in a way that's specific to his character. The economy is superb: four words to close out a visual gag that required 40 seconds of setup. Highly quotable and character-specific. This is close to an 8-anchor joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why is everyone just standing there like that? Did I miss something?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Are we doing a thing? Because I'm really good at things.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'I haven't seen my savings take a hit like this since I was a kid and they came up with Double Stuf Oreos.'
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are alarmed by their depleted bank statement
jokes.punchline: Chandler compares their financial crisis to the childhood trauma of Double Stuf Oreos being invented — implying he burned through his savings as a kid buying cookies
jokes.explanation: A charming, specific pop-culture reference that works because it's self-deprecating and reveals character (Chandler as a food-obsessed child). The specificity of 'Double Stuf Oreos' earns it. Not exceptional but above average for this type of joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: When I was a kid, I had $127 in my piggy bank. By the end of summer, I'd spent it all on Thin Mints.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'I'm inclined to blame Enron.'
jokes.setup: Monica asks what happened to all their money
jokes.punchline: Chandler deflects with an absurd but topical scapegoat — blaming Enron for their personal overspending
jokes.explanation: Topical joke (Enron scandal was 2001-2002) that lands on economy and self-aware evasion. The irony of blaming a corporate scandal for personal financial mismanagement is light but functional. Ages poorly without the cultural context.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't know exactly what happened to our money.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It must have been that corporate scandal. You know, the one that's happening right now.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Although it would be nice if the thing that you loved was finding gold.'
jokes.setup: Monica sincerely says she can't ask Chandler to give up something he loves doing (the internship)
jokes.punchline: She immediately qualifies her support by wishing his passion were more financially lucrative — specifically, gold-finding
jokes.explanation: Good character joke for Monica — her controlling, practical side undercuts her moment of generosity. The specificity of 'finding gold' (not just 'something lucrative') is the right level of absurd. The structure of setup-reversal is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I support you doing what you love, Chandler. I really do. I just wish your passion was more financially practical.

jokes.text: Monica suggests: 'Maybe we start eating out of Joey's refrigerator for a change.'
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler discuss cutting back expenses
jokes.punchline: Monica suggests raiding Joey's fridge — a running joke about Joey's enormous food consumption and his fridge being always stocked
jokes.explanation: Functional running-gag reference to Joey's food habits. Gets a mild laugh from fans of the show but doesn't add anything new to the joke. Competent but uninspired.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We need to cut back on expenses. Starting now, nobody touches the fridge without asking.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Nobody? Monica, I'm Joey Tribbiani. The fridge and I have an understanding.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, understand this: you're banned. From now on, I'm eating all your food.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: My food? Monica, I don't have food. That's the whole point.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Or, you slipped on ice at their house last month. Can we sue them?'
jokes.setup: Chandler suggests borrowing money from his parents as a worst-case scenario
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately pivots to suing them instead — revealing her mercenary practicality and the low quality of their relationship with the in-laws
jokes.explanation: Solid character moment — Monica's immediate pivot from 'borrow from parents' to 'sue parents' reveals something true about her personality and their family dynamic. The specificity that it happened 'last month' makes it funnier — she's been sitting on this idea.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, and what are we gonna find in there? A half-empty bottle of ketchup and a can of beans from 1987?

jokes.text: Chandler: 'If there's one thing my father taught me, it was... well, to always knock before going into the pool house.'
jokes.setup: Chandler begins to cite a paternal life lesson about pride and money
jokes.punchline: The lesson is about knocking before entering the pool house — implying he witnessed something traumatic/sexual there, a callback to Chandler's dysfunctional father (a Vegas drag performer)
jokes.explanation: One of the stronger jokes in the episode. The misdirection is well-structured — the setup promises wisdom, the punchline delivers dark family trauma wrapped in understatement. 'Pool house' is the perfect detail: affluent, specific, and implies just enough without explaining. Heavily character-integrated — only Chandler's history makes this land. The follow-up 'The other thing is, never borrow money' restores the original thread perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We could borrow from my parents.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Or we could sue them and make a lot more money.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'I am your man. I'm gonna get us through this situation... even if it means you working twice as hard.'
jokes.setup: Chandler delivers a macho declaration of taking charge of their financial problems
jokes.punchline: His solution is for Monica to work harder — completely undermining his masculine posturing
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler self-undermining bravado. The structure is clean — build up the man speech, then immediately hand the burden to Monica. Character-specific in that Chandler's blustering incompetence is well-established. Lands reliably.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: My father taught me something very important. He said, 'Son, if you ever find yourself in an awkward situation, just leave the room.'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's it. That's the wisdom. Get out. Don't stay, don't try to fix it, just go.

jokes.text: Joey watching nature documentary: 'You don't like eating animals, but you love watching them tear each other apart.' Joey: 'No, I don't-- Get him. Get him!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe calls out Joey's hypocrisy about loving violent animal documentaries
jokes.punchline: Joey begins to deny it but immediately gets sucked back into the TV, shouting encouragement at the predator
jokes.explanation: Well-timed physical/reaction comedy. Joey's inability to control his own hypocrisy mid-sentence is perfectly in character. The mid-denial cutoff to 'Get him! Get him!' is the right comedic beat and structure. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'll be the man and get us through this.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: How?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You work harder.

jokes.text: Joey watching nature doc: 'Separate the sick one from the herd!'
jokes.setup: Joey is already shouting at the TV at the predator
jokes.punchline: He continues with specific, strategic wildlife advice — as if coaching a sports team — escalating his investment in the kill
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of joke #12. The tactical detail ('separate the sick one from the herd') elevates the absurdity — Joey is now coaching predators like a football play. Character-consistent and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: You love watching animals fight.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I do not!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Come on, the mantis is totally gonna take him down!

jokes.text: Joey: 'I put that tube top on as a joke.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe says she has something that'll fit Joey so he doesn't have to go home for clothes
jokes.punchline: Joey has apparently already tried on the tube top — 'as a joke' — but the fact that he needs to clarify this implies it looked good or he considered wearing it
jokes.explanation: Economical and funny. The audience never sees the tube top moment — it happened off-screen — but Joey's defensive 'as a joke' implies everything. The ambiguity (did he look good in it? did he consider keeping it on?) is funnier than showing it. Joey's casual relationship with gender norms is character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I have some clothes you could wear.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, that's so sweet! Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Yeah, well... I tried on your tube top.

jokes.text: Joey: 'I've got as much use out of these boxers as I can.' / Rachel: 'Why don't you turn them inside--' / Joey: 'Done it.'
jokes.setup: Joey says he needs to go home because his boxers are worn out
jokes.punchline: Rachel's suggestion about turning them inside-out is cut off because Joey already did it — implying he's been wearing the same underwear long enough to need that trick
jokes.explanation: Very well-structured joke. The cutoff before Rachel finishes the sentence — answered by 'Done it' — is perfect economy. The two-word punchline conveys an entire gross backstory without elaborating. Character-perfect for Joey's slovenly lifestyle. The rhythm (interrupted question → one-word answer) is textbook sitcom timing.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: He's already turned them inside out

jokes.text: Joey, still bleeding from the animal: 'Oh, fine. Yeah, you got away. But don't look so smug. You're gonna bleed to death.'
jokes.setup: Joey was bleeding from something (implied animal bite/scratch) while watching nature docs
jokes.punchline: He trash-talks the escaped animal with a death threat — 'you're gonna bleed to death' — projecting onto the creature while he himself is bleeding
jokes.explanation: Callback to the opening scene pays off with a satisfying absurdist button. Joey threatening an escaped animal while himself bleeding is both character-perfect and logically absurd. The 'don't look so smug' address to an animal is a funny anthropomorphization.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Come on, little guy, you can make it! Run, run, run! Oh my God, no! No, no, no! You're so slow! The cheetah is gonna get you! Why are you running toward the rocks? That's stupid! Go left! LEFT! Oh, you idiot, now you're trapped!

jokes.text: Joey: 'I hate going back to my apartment now. Partly because I live above a known crack den...'
jokes.setup: Joey says he doesn't want to go back to his apartment
jokes.punchline: He cites living above a 'known crack den' as a reason — mentioned so casually it implies this is a totally normal thing to him
jokes.explanation: The casualness of 'known crack den' is the joke — it's a Phoebe-and-Joey style acknowledgment of their chaotic downtown lives. Works as a quick laugh but isn't particularly crafted; the comedy is entirely in the delivery of the mundane qualifier 'known.'

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I hate going home. My stepfather's always there.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I live above a drug dealer. And I have to go home to my wife.

jokes.text: Phoebe fantasizes aloud: 'Pick up your socks. Put down the toilet seat. No, we are not having sex anymore.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe excitedly says she's always wanted to live with a guy
jokes.punchline: She imagines the clichéd complaints of cohabitation — culminating in 'No, we are not having sex anymore' — apparently her idea of domestic bliss
jokes.explanation: The escalating list of cohabitation complaints is a recognizable observational beat, but the punchline 'No, we are not having sex anymore' subverts it nicely — she's looking forward to the full domestic experience including its downsides. Phoebe-specific in its earnestness.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, yes! I want to move in with you!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I want to wake up next to you, and fall asleep next to you, and spend the rest of my life with you.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: But I'm keeping my apartment because I think it's bad luck to give up an apartment in New York.

jokes.text: Joey, shirtless, yelling at TV: 'Shame on you, TV Guide. A man's ass is not nudity!'
jokes.setup: Scene cut to Joey alone watching TV
jokes.punchline: Joey is outraged at TV Guide's modesty standards regarding male nudity — which is both character-specific (Joey's vanity/comfort with his body) and absurdly specific
jokes.explanation: Underrated joke. 'A man's ass is not nudity!' is a great standalone line — specific, outraged, and perfectly Joey. His casual relationship with bodies and his actor's vanity inform this completely. The 'TV Guide' specificity dates it charmingly. The cold cut-to of Joey making this proclamation alone in his apartment is visually funny even from the transcript.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I've always wanted to live with a guy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: He never puts the toilet seat down, he leaves his socks everywhere, and he's always watching sports on TV instead of paying attention to me.

jokes.text: Joey immediately interprets Monica's secret request as her wanting to have an affair with him: 'I'd be lying if I said I hadn't thought about it myself. But Chandler is my best friend. It would be wrong. Good, but wrong.'
jokes.setup: Monica asks Joey to keep something secret from Chandler
jokes.punchline: Joey's stream of consciousness assumes she wants to sleep with him — and he delivers a whole internal moral deliberation before she clarifies
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The extended internal monologue Joey delivers — unprompted — where he works through the morality of sleeping with Monica ('Good, but wrong') is perfectly character-integrated. It requires no setup beyond Monica's vague phrasing. Joey's self-flattery ('I'd be lying if I said I hadn't thought about it myself') adds another layer. The structure of letting Joey go through the whole arc before correcting him is textbook slow-burn sitcom comedy. The punchline 'Good, but wrong' is immediately quotable. Approaches the 8-anchor threshold.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? It's not a big deal. Guys show their butts all the time on TV. Women don't want to see that anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But when a woman shows her butt, suddenly it's 'controversial' and 'we need to alert the sponsors.' It's a double standard!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A man's rear end is a thing of beauty. It's art. It's natural. Why are we ashamed of the male form?

jokes.text: Monica: 'I need to borrow some money.' / Joey: 'Oh, I don't know, Monica. Lending friends money is always a mistake.' / Monica: 'But Chandler lent you money.' / Joey: 'And he would tell you it was a mistake.'
jokes.setup: Monica asks Joey for a loan
jokes.punchline: Joey cites the principle that lending friends money is a mistake — but confirms it by volunteering that Chandler learned this lesson from lending Joey money
jokes.explanation: Smart structure: Joey's self-incrimination to prove his point is funny and reveals character. The irony that his best evidence for the principle is his own behavior is well-landed. Joey being oblivious to his own hypocrisy here is character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, I need to ask you something about Chandler. It's kind of personal.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Monica, I'm flattered, but I don't think Chandler would be cool with this.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? No! I just wanted to know—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Look, you're a beautiful woman, but my boy Chandler is my best friend. I can't do that to him.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, you're not listening to me!

jokes.text: Monica: 'What do you think I am, a soap opera star?' / Joey: 'Yeah.' / [beat] / Joey: 'That's right, I am.'
jokes.setup: Monica balks at the $2000 amount she's asking for
jokes.punchline: Joey affirms Monica's rhetorical question literally (he IS a soap opera star), then has to remind himself of this fact — a beat of Joey not quite keeping up with his own life
jokes.explanation: Very well-timed reaction beat. Joey answering a rhetorical question literally is character-specific (his literalness is a consistent trait), but the extra beat of 'That's right, I am' — where he has to remind himself — is the real joke. The self-discovery element gives it an extra dimension. Economical and character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But it would still be great!

jokes.text: Monica: 'It'll really hurt his pride.' / Joey: 'Chandler? Pride?' [pause] 'I know, he thinks he has it. It's really cute.'
jokes.setup: Monica worries borrowing money will hurt Chandler's pride
jokes.punchline: Joey's confusion at the concept of Chandler having pride — followed by the patronizing 'he thinks he has it, it's really cute' — frames Chandler as delusional about his own toughness
jokes.explanation: Genuinely good joke. 'He thinks he has it. It's really cute.' reframes Chandler's pride as a child-like illusion that friends humor. Joey's fondness is genuine, which makes the dismissiveness funnier. 'It's really cute' is a strong button. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, can you lend me $2000?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Monica, do I look like I have $2000?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait... I'm on a TV show. I make like $20,000 an episode. Oh my God, I'm rich!

jokes.text: Joey: 'When I was a kid, it was like: Whoops, Joey fell down the stairs. Or, Whoops, Joey electrocuted himself again.'
jokes.setup: Ross explains he's baby-proofing the apartment because Emma has started crawling
jokes.punchline: Joey recalls his own childhood safety as a cavalier shrug — the word 'again' on 'electrocuted himself again' implying this was a repeated occurrence
jokes.explanation: 'Again' is the key word doing all the work — it implies this was routine, not a one-off incident. Dark but not too dark, perfectly framed through Joey's breezy nostalgia. Character-specific: explains a lot about adult Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It would hurt Chandler's pride.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Chandler's pride? That's adorable.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'You don't think a woman can do this?' / Joey: 'Women can. You can't.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is offended that Joey is skeptical about her ability to baby-proof the apartment herself
jokes.punchline: Joey sidesteps the sexism charge by making it personal — not a gender issue, specifically a Rachel issue
jokes.explanation: Economically brilliant. Five words do two things at once: defuse the sexism accusation AND deliver a harsher insult. The structure is perfect — the pivot from general to specific is the joke. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, parents today are crazy with all this baby-proofing stuff. Corner guards, outlet covers, gates everywhere. It's insane!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I grew up without any of that and I turned out fine. Sure, I fell down the stairs a few times, got my head stuck in the bannister once, swallowed a whole bottle of vitamins... but look at me! I'm great!

jokes.text: Rachel: 'What? Come on, I found the hardware store all by myself.' / Joey: 'The store's right down the street.' / Rachel: 'There is a hardware store right down the street?'
jokes.setup: Rachel defends her competence by saying she found the hardware store
jokes.punchline: The store is literally on the same block — and Rachel didn't know this, confirming Joey's low assessment of her
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff to joke #26. Rachel's self-undermining revelation proves Joey right immediately. The three-beat structure (Rachel's defense → Joey's correction → Rachel's clueless response) is clean sitcom architecture. Rachel's 'There is a hardware store?' is a great character-specific oblivious line.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Do you think women can't do handiwork?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, I think you can't do handiwork.

jokes.text: Mike: 'Well, it's just like living with a girl, only they don't steal your makeup. Unless they're playing This Is What My Sister Would Look Like.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe says she's never lived with a guy before
jokes.punchline: Mike says guys don't steal makeup — then self-undermines with the revelation that he has played 'This Is What My Sister Would Look Like' in drag, implying a troubled relationship with his sister
jokes.explanation: Good self-undermining joke. 'This Is What My Sister Would Look Like' is a funny game name and the specificity implies a whole weird backstory Mike isn't elaborating on. Character-specific for Mike's slightly dark, deadpan humor.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I found the hardware store all by myself! I'm so proud of me.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's great, Rach. Where is it?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's right next to Pottery Barn.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, that's two blocks away. There's one right on the corner of our street.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What?!

jokes.text: Mike: 'Yeah, she's not so cute.' [about his sister/himself in makeup]
jokes.setup: Mike has revealed he dressed in his sister's makeup
jokes.punchline: His verdict on his own appearance in drag is delivered with flat resignation: 'She's not so cute'
jokes.explanation: Button on the previous joke. 'Not so cute' is a good deadpan button — the economy is excellent. Works best as an extension of #28.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Guys don't steal makeup like girls do.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I use makeup to imagine my sister.

jokes.text: Phoebe tells Mike to put the toilet seat down. Mike says 'Yes, dear.' Monica asks if it's a bit. Rachel: 'Uh-huh. We're playing you two.'
jokes.setup: Mike's reflexive 'Yes, dear' to Phoebe prompts Monica to ask if it's a scripted bit
jokes.punchline: Rachel confirms they're doing an impression of Monica and Chandler's relationship dynamic — suggesting Phoebe already bosses Mike around like Monica does Chandler
jokes.explanation: Good group comedy moment. The meta-twist that Mike/Phoebe are unknowingly mimicking Monica/Chandler's dynamic is a solid group character joke. Monica's defensive 'We don't do that' followed by Chandler's 'Yes, dear' is a perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So what's your domestic routine like with Mike?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, we're just consciously parodying Monica and Chandler.

jokes.text: Monica: 'We don't do that. Tell her we don't do that.' / Chandler: 'Yes, dear.'
jokes.setup: Monica denies that she and Chandler have the 'Yes, dear' dynamic
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately confirms the joke by saying 'Yes, dear' to Monica's demand that he defend them
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect joke structure. Monica's denial requires Chandler to prove it wrong — and he does so immediately and perfectly by using the exact phrase she's denying. The irony is completely self-generating. Practically no words needed. This is excellent sitcom architecture — the joke proves itself without explanation. One of the episode's strongest.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Your eyes are very blue.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Thanks.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm not gay. I just have eyes. And they work.

jokes.text: Ross about Mike: 'I mean, he's a great catch. And those eyes....' [pause] 'I'm a scientist. I observe.'
jokes.setup: Ross is complimenting Mike to Phoebe in a standard 'you got a good one' way
jokes.punchline: He drifts into appreciating Mike's eyes, catches himself in what sounds like attraction, then retreats to 'I'm a scientist. I observe.' as a defense
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'I'm a scientist. I observe.' is immediately quotable and funny on multiple levels: it's Ross's pomposity being deployed to cover an awkward moment, the deflection is completely inadequate as a cover, and it reveals Ross noticing another man's attractiveness without being willing to admit it. The pause before the justification does real comedic work. Character-perfect: only Ross would pivot to his professional identity here. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I want my wedding dress to have a neckline that says, 'I'm a bride, but I'm also a woman who knows what she wants.' You know, something that really showcases the girls, but in a classy way. Like, they should have their own spotlight, but they're still part of the ensemble cast.

jokes.text: Phoebe fantasizes about her wedding dress: '...that highlights my breasts in an obvious yet classy way.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe describes her hypothetical wedding in increasingly conventional terms
jokes.punchline: The wedding dress specification — 'highlights my breasts in an obvious yet classy way' — is the perfect Phoebe qualifier: earthy and specific in a way that undercuts the fantasy's elegance
jokes.explanation: 'Obvious yet classy' is the right pairing of contradictory adjectives — specific to Phoebe's self-image and her blend of earthiness and aspiration. Character-specific and well-phrased.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know what? I've been thinking. I want a normal life. A real family. A house in the suburbs with a white picket fence and 2.5 kids and a minivan and a golden retriever named Buddy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, that's wonderful!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I'm gonna bake cookies and drive carpool and volunteer at the PTA and wear those velvet tracksuits and drink wine from a giant goblet while I watch my stories.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's... very specific.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And I'm gonna name my minivan something cute like 'The Pheebus' and put those stick figure family decals on the back window, and every morning I'll say 'Have a great day at school, honey!' even if they're thirty years old.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Oh, my God, load up the Volvo, I want to be a soccer mom.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe realizes she's fantasizing about a completely conventional domestic life — house in Connecticut, kids named Sophie and Mike Jr.
jokes.punchline: Her embrace of the ultimate suburban cliché ('load up the Volvo') is funny because it's so completely at odds with Phoebe's established free-spirit identity
jokes.explanation: Good character-subversion joke. 'Load up the Volvo' is the perfect specific symbol of suburban domesticity — not just any car, specifically a Volvo. The specificity earns it. Phoebe wanting to be a soccer mom is funny because of who Phoebe is.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, did you just call her 'roomie'? That's so cute. You guys are like... groombies!

jokes.text: Mike: 'Don't you mean groomie?' / Phoebe: 'Honey, leave the terrible jokes to me.'
jokes.setup: Mike makes a wordplay joke on 'roomie' — 'don't you mean groomie?'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe calls it out as a terrible joke and tells Mike to leave bad jokes to her — a meta-acknowledgment that Phoebe makes famously bad jokes and this is beneath even her standards
jokes.explanation: Smart meta-joke. The layering works: Mike makes a genuinely bad pun, Phoebe calls it terrible, and the callback to Phoebe being the established bad-joke maker adds self-awareness. 'Leave the terrible jokes to me' is a funny assertion of her ownership over bad humor.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm like your groomie!

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: That's a good one. I wish I could come up with stuff like that. All I ever do is make stupid jokes.

jokes.text: Mike's talking-head: 'We haven't even moved in yet, and they have us picking out china patterns.' [pause] 'China patterns!'
jokes.setup: Mike is processing the rapid escalation from moving-in to wedding planning
jokes.punchline: The repeated 'China patterns!' — said with the scandalized horror of a man confronting his worst fear — is the button
jokes.explanation: Standard 'commitment-phobic man reacting to domesticity' joke. The repeated 'China patterns!' is a decent button but the concept isn't fresh. Gets a mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't know what I'm doing. I tried to put this safety gate up and it just... fell down. Twice. I think I bent it.

jokes.text: Rachel trying to baby-proof: 'This is easy. Can't do this....' [repeated failure, visual gag]
jokes.setup: Rachel confidently says she'll install the baby-proofing herself after Joey and Monica both doubted her
jokes.punchline: Extended visual sequence of Rachel completely failing at the basic installation task — proving Joey and Monica correct
jokes.explanation: Functional physical callback to the earlier doubts about Rachel's handywoman skills. The visual gag pays off the setup but isn't particularly inventive — it's just the expected result of the earlier joke. The two-stage narration ('This is easy' then 'Wow, seriously. Can't do this.') gives it a mild escalation but the material itself is predictable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. So you're broke?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wow. I figured that out all by myself!

jokes.text: Chandler, surprised Joey already knew about the money trouble: 'What? What do you mean, you know?' / Joey: 'I just figured it out... I mean, you're not working, and the economy is bad.' / Chandler: 'Oh, right. That is the fastest I have ever thought.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is shocked Joey already guessed their financial situation
jokes.punchline: Joey's reasoning is so obvious ('you're not working and the economy is bad') that Chandler, in genuine awe, calls it 'the fastest I have ever thought' — revealing how low his baseline for Joey's reasoning is
jokes.explanation: Good Chandler-Joey dynamic joke. 'That is the fastest I have ever thought' is the right delivery — Chandler's sincere amazement at the most elementary logic is a great character beat. Reveals both Chandler's low expectations for Joey and Joey's smug satisfaction.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I got it right! I got it right!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: How did I do that? How did I know that?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm like a genius or something!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, what were we talking about?

jokes.text: Joey guesses the exact amount Chandler needs to borrow ($2000). Chandler: 'Yes, $2000 exactly. How did you know that?' / Joey explains rent math. / Chandler: 'Oh, okay. I am on fire.'
jokes.setup: Joey preemptively names the exact dollar amount Chandler needs and explains his reasoning
jokes.punchline: Chandler's response — 'I am on fire' — is delivered with the same excessive pride over elementary arithmetic as before, escalating his amazement at Joey's most basic reasoning
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the previous joke. Joey's self-congratulation builds nicely. The parallel structure (first 'fastest I've ever thought,' now 'I am on fire') gives the running gag a satisfying shape.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A lot of stuff.

jokes.text: Chandler sees Joey's check register: 'Did you write a check to Monica for $2000?' — realizing both he and Monica independently borrowed money from Joey and each swore the other to secrecy
jokes.setup: Both Chandler and Monica separately went to Joey for secret loans, each telling Joey not to tell the other
jokes.punchline: Chandler discovers Monica's check while getting his own — the structural irony of both spouses doing the same shameful thing surfaces simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed plot payoff. The irony that both Chandler and Monica went to Joey for the same loan with the same secrecy clause is a solid structural joke. The escalation of shame — both caught doing the thing they criticized — is satisfying sitcom architecture.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica doesn't need a boob job.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, what would be crazy is if she got a butt job.

jokes.text: Joey, after Chandler asks what Monica could've spent $2000 on that she'd keep secret: 'Boob job.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is puzzled about what Monica would spend $2000 on secretly
jokes.punchline: Joey delivers 'Boob job' with complete confidence and zero hesitation
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word punchline. The economy is flawless — after Chandler's long, worried speculation, Joey answers immediately with zero uncertainty. 'Boob job' lands as the episode's title payoff and immediately triggers the whole second-act misunderstanding. The confidence of the delivery (no buildup, no hedging) is what makes it land. Character-perfect for Joey, who would genuinely think this is the obvious answer. One of the episode's best single moments.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Do you have a porn stash?

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: No, I don't have a porn stash.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: It's in the desk drawer under the instruction manuals.

jokes.text: Joey: 'She was afraid you wouldn't be supportive.' / Chandler: 'I'm not.' / Joey: 'She knows you well.'
jokes.setup: Joey (falsely) explains Monica wanted a boob job and feared Chandler wouldn't support it
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately confirms he's not supportive — and Joey affirms 'she knows you well' — landing as a character indictment of Chandler while also being factually wrong
jokes.explanation: Tight three-line exchange. 'She knows you well' is a quietly devastating button — Joey's neutrality combined with the accidental truth (Chandler IS unsupportive, just not about this) makes it sting. Great economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: A 'groomie'? That's a play on words — 'groom' and 'roomie.' Get it? Because I'm the groom, and you're my roomie. So 'groomie.'

jokes.text: Joey: 'Well, it's not that crazy, okay? Making them smaller, that would be crazy.'
jokes.setup: Chandler says a boob job is 'crazy'
jokes.punchline: Joey concedes the point but specifies that REDUCTION would be crazy — a classic Joey body-part-focused value judgment
jokes.explanation: Good Joey-specific logic. His prioritization hierarchy (bigger = good, smaller = unthinkable) is perfectly in character. 'That would be crazy' as a deadpan absolute is funny because of its certainty.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wow, Mike, that's so funny! Oh my God, I get it now! It's like 'groom' and 'homie' put together! Wow, you're so smart!

jokes.text: Joey, back at Phoebe's, immediately: 'Hey, so where do you keep your secret box of porn?' / Phoebe: 'I don't have any porn.' / Joey: 'Back of the closet in my bedroom.'
jokes.setup: Joey arrives at Phoebe's apartment and immediately asks about porn
jokes.punchline: Phoebe denies having porn; Joey immediately answers with the exact location — revealing he already knew the answer to his own question
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: Joey asks where the porn is, Phoebe denies having it, Joey answers his own question with pinpoint specificity. This implies Joey has already found Phoebe's porn and was just doing a weird social ritual of asking. The specificity ('back of the closet in my bedroom') is crucial — it's not a guess, it's knowledge. Perfectly character-integrated for Joey. High economy and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Yeah, my wife, she's... she's really into extreme sports. Last week she went skydiving without a parachute.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh. That's... that's not good.

jokes.text: 'I don't have any porn.' / 'Back of the closet in my bedroom.'
jokes.setup: Joey asks where Chandler's secret porn is kept.
jokes.punchline: Chandler denies having any porn — then immediately provides the exact location of his porn.
jokes.explanation: A beautiful two-beat structure: denial immediately followed by the specific answer to the denied question. The gap between 'I don't have any porn' and 'back of the closet in my bedroom' is the entire joke — Chandler can't hold the lie for even a sentence. The specificity ('back of the closet') adds to the comedy because it shows exactly how well-located the supposedly non-existent item is. Structurally near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, maybe he'd feel differently if he was with someone else. I mean, I'm not perfect. I have one exception to perfect toilet behavior.

jokes.text: Mike: 'I get the joke. Sophisticated as it was.'
jokes.setup: Joey explains to Mike that the 'groomie' joke works because it's a play on 'roomie'
jokes.punchline: Mike sarcastically thanks Joey for the explanation of the joke he made, adding 'sophisticated as it was' — skewering Joey's condescending explanation and his own bad joke simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Good dry retort. Mike's deadpan delivery of 'sophisticated as it was' does two things: mocks his own joke and deflates Joey's pompous explanation. Economical and character-appropriate for Mike's dry humor.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I called, but I couldn't figure out how to use the baby gates. I mean, I can't even use chopsticks.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You can't use chopsticks?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No! I always just end up eating a lot really fast and then crying.

jokes.text: Mike: 'At one point, near the end, she deliberately defecated on my--' / Phoebe: 'Okay, well, that's bad. Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Mike explains his first marriage was a disaster and starts to give a specific example
jokes.punchline: The sentence is cut off before completion — but the beginning ('deliberately defecated on my--') is enough to make clear this was a profound violation, and the cutoff makes it funnier than any completion could
jokes.explanation: Excellent cutoff joke. The interrupted sentence is funnier than any completion because the audience fills in the worst possible ending themselves. 'Deliberately' is the key word — it wasn't accidental. 'Defecated on my--' with the cutoff is a masterclass in comedic economy: it implies a horrifying specific story, invites imagination, and Phoebe's flat 'Okay, well, that's bad. Yeah.' is the perfect understated response. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Phoebe: '...a blond who always uses the toilet?' / [beat] / Phoebe: 'Except for once in the ocean.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is trying to convince Mike that marriage might be better with the right person — specifically her — and pitches herself as someone who 'always uses the toilet'
jokes.punchline: She immediately qualifies this with the exception — 'once in the ocean' — which she mentions completely casually
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The callback structure is perfect: Phoebe pitches herself as the toilet-using alternative to Mike's ex-wife, then immediately undermines her own pitch with 'except for once in the ocean' — delivered with zero shame. The ocean exception is Phoebe-specific: casual, oddly specific, and reveals a whole unspoken story. The deadpan delivery of a confessional that explains nothing makes it perfect. High quotability and rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I wouldn't change anything about Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, there are two things...

jokes.text: Handyman arriving at Rachel's: 'Hi. So you gave in and decided to call someone?' / Rachel: 'Yeah. I don't know who I was kidding. I can barely use chopsticks.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has given up on the baby-proofing and called a professional
jokes.punchline: Rachel's self-assessment — 'I can barely use chopsticks' as a measure of her manual dexterity — is the perfect specific detail for her character and social class
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff. 'I can barely use chopsticks' is the right class-specific measure of uselessness for Rachel — she doesn't say she can't use tools, she cites chopsticks, which reveals her entire upbringing in one image. Character-specific and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Your eyes are like... like two brown... things. And your skin is... smooth. And your legs go all the way up and make a butt.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Did you just say my legs go all the way up and make a butt?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I was going for poetry. How'd I do?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You did great.

jokes.text: Ross to Rachel: 'Hey, Rach. There she is, my perfectly proportioned wife.'
jokes.setup: Ross enters trying to subtly reassure Rachel that he doesn't want her body to change — having misunderstood that she's getting a boob job
jokes.punchline: 'Perfectly proportioned wife' — said with the forced enthusiasm of a man trying to preemptively talk someone out of a surgery he doesn't understand
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the extended misunderstanding sequence. Gets a mild laugh from the forced compliment energy. The real comedy is yet to come.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Do you want any part of me to get bigger?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh! Um... no.

jokes.text: Rachel (to camera/aside): 'Don't look at me. I never get his jokes.'
jokes.setup: Ross delivers the bizarrely elaborate 'perfectly proportioned wife' compliment
jokes.punchline: Rachel's aside — 'I never get his jokes' — implies she assumes this is a bit, not a sincere (if weird) compliment
jokes.explanation: Decent reaction beat — Rachel's dismissal of Ross's odd behavior as 'his jokes' is character-appropriate and gets a mild laugh. Functions as a bridge to the bigger misunderstanding to come.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, what are you doing? First you're staring at her, then you're following her around the apartment, now you're smelling her hair?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I was just—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I'm calling it. You've gone full creepy. You're like one restraining order away from being a guy on the news.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Do you know there is not one thing I would change about you? Not one single thing. And definitely not... two single things.'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to convince Rachel not to get a boob job without revealing he knows
jokes.punchline: 'Definitely not... two single things' — a barely-veiled reference to her breasts that completely undermines his speech
jokes.explanation: Good wordplay and misdirection. The switch from 'one thing' to 'two single things' is the punchline, and the audience gets it immediately. The cascade from sincere compliment to unintentional breast reference is structurally clean. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So when you say 'don't get bigger,' you mean like my clothes?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no, I just meant—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Because that's what my high school volleyball coach used to say right before he'd make us run laps in our underwear.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'Okay, you're being weird. Do you want sex, or did you do something bad?'
jokes.setup: Ross is delivering increasingly bizarre, over-effusive compliments
jokes.punchline: Rachel has a simple two-category explanation for a man acting overly nice
jokes.explanation: Sharp observational line. 'Do you want sex, or did you do something bad?' is a compact and recognizable relationship truth — men have two reasons to be over-nice. Good economy and high quotability. Character-appropriate for Rachel's directness.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And then there's the swelling, the mood swings, the incredible pain... but it's all magical!

jokes.text: Ross: 'I am warm... for your form.'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to compliment Rachel's body without revealing what he knows
jokes.punchline: 'Warm for your form' — a rhyming slang phrase that's both a failed attempt at cool and an accidentally lewd expression
jokes.explanation: Good Ross-specific cringe wordplay. 'Warm for your form' is exactly what Ross would say when trying to be suave — rhyming slang that makes him sound desperate. Character-integrated and mildly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, the man who's been married three times is an expert on love.

jokes.text: 'I am warm... for your form.'
jokes.setup: Monica challenges Chandler to explain his compliments. He tries to say he loves how she looks.
jokes.punchline: Chandler deploys 'warm for your form' — a rhyming slang-style declaration that is simultaneously dorky, endearing, and transparently inadequate as a cover for his panic.
jokes.explanation: The rhyme 'warm for your form' is Chandler's verbal tic under pressure — he retreats to wordplay when cornered. Character-consistent and mildly amusing. The dorky rhyme implies he's scrambling. Good character integration, modest originality.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's not 'Divorce-o,' it's 'Relationship Researcher.' I'm conducting a longitudinal study on the dissolution of romantic partnerships.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Divorce-o.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I prefer 'Serial Commitment Analyst.'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Or you could just go with 'Three-Time Loser.'

jokes.text: Rachel: 'Okay, you know the old classics like, you know, You look nice? They're still okay.'
jokes.setup: Ross's bizarre compliments prompt Rachel to give him pointers
jokes.punchline: Rachel suggests the radical idea of just saying 'you look nice' — framing basic compliments as classics Ross has abandoned
jokes.explanation: Light callback to Ross's bizarre complimenting. Works as connective tissue but isn't a standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: We had some really good times before she came out.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And some really good times after.

jokes.text: Ross: 'I mean, I wouldn't want anything to get any bigger.' / [pause] 'Don't answer that.'
jokes.setup: Ross asks Rachel if she'd want any part of him to get bigger — fishing to see if she agrees with the 'no changes' philosophy — then realizes what he's opened the door to
jokes.punchline: 'Don't answer that' — the rapid self-correction implies he suddenly realized he doesn't want to know the answer
jokes.explanation: Good self-aware beat. Ross's rapid self-correction ('Don't answer that') implies he realized the question could be answered unflattering ways about his own body. The beat between the question and the retraction is the joke. Economical.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: The Divorcer. That's my nickname.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That's the saddest thing I've ever heard.

jokes.text: Rachel's talking-head: 'Just when you thought that dude couldn't get any weirder.'
jokes.setup: Ross's bizarre compliment session just ended
jokes.punchline: Rachel's flat assessment of her baby-daddy: 'that dude'
jokes.explanation: Functional talking-head reaction. 'That dude' as a descriptor for the father of her child is mildly funny but the line itself isn't particularly crafted. Gets a small laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, thank you. I love them too. I mean, what's not to love? They're like two little... I don't know, two little... okay, fine, they're breasts. But they're MY breasts, and I'm happy with them.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know you are. And I love them exactly the way they are.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? That's very sweet, but I'm thinking about getting them done.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What?! No! Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Because everyone in this city has them done!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Rachel, that's like saying everyone's jumping off the Brooklyn Bridge, so you should too.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That's different.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How is that different?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Because nobody would see them jumping off the Brooklyn Bridge!

jokes.text: Rachel: 'He sounded just like my high-school wrestling coach.'
jokes.setup: Rachel and Monica are discussing Ross's body-conscious comments ('No bigger, you're perfect, just don't get any bigger')
jokes.punchline: Rachel's unexpected association — her high-school wrestling coach — implies a very specific and strange memory, and suggests the wrestling coach was also obsessed with the girls' body size
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific non-sequitur. The specificity of 'wrestling coach' is unexpected and creates an entire implied backstory. It's also a great misdirection — we expect 'controlling boyfriend' and get 'wrestling coach.' Character-specific for Rachel's privileged private school world.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Your ass is gonna get bigger?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's one of the side effects of pregnancy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, could you do me a favor? Could you not?

jokes.text: Monica explaining pregnancy changes: 'Of course your body's gonna change. Your breasts are gonna get bigger, your ass is gonna get bigger... you're gonna lose bladder control.' / [pause] / 'God, it's just such a magical time.'
jokes.setup: Monica is trying to reassure Rachel about Ross's attitude toward pregnancy body changes
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from flattering changes (bigger breasts) to progressively undignified ones (bladder control loss), capped with Monica's sincere/ironic 'God, it's just such a magical time'
jokes.explanation: Good escalating list joke. The pivot from 'bigger breasts' to 'bladder control' is an effective descent into indignity. 'God, it's just such a magical time' works as either sincere or sarcastic — the ambiguity is the joke. Character-appropriate for Monica's brusque honesty.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, if I had to choose between having breasts and being bald, I guess I could live with the breasts.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? I'm just saying, at least I could wear a really nice sweater!

jokes.text: Ross to Phoebe, re: being asked about marriage: 'Now you're seeking me out to make jokes? I mean, I can see if we're all hanging out, but to come to my home....'
jokes.setup: Phoebe comes to Ross for marriage advice — he initially assumes she's there to mock his divorce record
jokes.punchline: Ross has apparently accepted that people come to him specifically to make divorce jokes — the horror is that he has a policy about it
jokes.explanation: Good self-aware Ross joke. The fact that he has a protocol for divorce jokes ('I can see if we're all hanging out, but to come to my home') implies this is so frequent he's developed rules around it. Character-perfect: Ross's wounded dignity is a core trait.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know, after hearing all these stories about childbirth, I'm starting to get a little nervous.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? Why would you be nervous? It's just... pushing a watermelon through a—

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God!

jokes.text: Ross: 'If you want to see a man gain weight and a woman stop shaving, get them married.'
jokes.setup: Ross initially agrees to tell Phoebe marriage is terrible
jokes.punchline: His pitch for marriage-being-bad involves both spouses letting themselves go in gender-specific ways
jokes.explanation: Generic observational joke about marriage. The 'man gets fat, woman stops shaving' bit is well-worn material. Functions here but not particularly fresh or character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. So you're telling me you borrowed all that money and didn't even get the boobs?

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Seriously, you? Divorce-o?' / Ross: 'If you have to call me a name, I'd prefer Ross, the Divorcer. It's just cooler.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is surprised Ross loves marriage given his track record
jokes.punchline: Ross's rebranding of his divorce identity — 'Ross, the Divorcer' — with the aesthetic note 'it's just cooler' is perfectly vain and self-deluded
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Ross, the Divorcer. It's just cooler.' reveals everything about his character: his desperate need to control his own narrative, his pomposity, and his obliviousness. The preference for a superhero-esque title for his divorces is perfectly Ross. The 'it's just cooler' justification is what elevates this from a good joke to a great one — he has an aesthetic opinion about his own humiliation. High quotability and rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I've got it. From now on, when people ask me about my divorces, I'm going to tell them I'm not divorced... I'm 'serially committed.'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's not better.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What about 'marriage enthusiast'?

jokes.text: Ross: 'Carol and I had some good times before she became a lesbian. And once afterward.'
jokes.setup: Ross is listing positive examples of his marriages
jokes.punchline: 'And once afterward' — a one-phrase reveal that he and Carol had sex at least once after she came out as a lesbian, delivered with casual casualness
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy joke. 'And once afterward' implies an enormous and complicated backstory in three words. The casualness of its delivery — appended almost as an afterthought — is what makes it great. It suggests Ross is either clueless or weirdly proud of this fact, and the ambiguity is funnier than clarity would be. High quotability. One of the episode's genuinely exceptional moments.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can see myself in a Volvo. I'm driving through the woods, listening to NPR, and there's a dead body in the back.

jokes.text: Ross to Phoebe: 'The Divorcer to the rescue.' / Phoebe: 'It's not cooler.' / Ross: 'Yeah, I just heard it.'
jokes.setup: Ross uses his new superhero divorce title after giving Phoebe advice
jokes.punchline: Phoebe calls it not cooler; Ross immediately agrees: 'Yeah, I just heard it' — the callback makes him realize in real time that his new branding doesn't work
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff. 'Yeah, I just heard it' is the right self-aware response — Ross's real-time brand evaluation is funny. The structure of the callback is clean and the self-correction is character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Moving is so easy, right?

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, piece of cake. My back only feels like it's been hit by a truck.

jokes.text: Monica, using tools: 'So I can't do anything I like?!' [extended visual of Monica failing at baby-proofing]
jokes.setup: Monica, a professional chef who confidently said she could baby-proof the apartment herself, is now struggling
jokes.punchline: Monica — who normally excels at everything domestic — fails at the hardware task, mirroring the Rachel visual gag from earlier
jokes.explanation: Weaker callback. Rachel failing at baby-proofing was funny because it confirmed the earlier jokes about her specifically being incompetent. Monica failing at it removes the character specificity — Monica is usually competent — and the visual gag lacks the same precision. The line 'So I can't do anything I like?!' is weaker comedy writing. Below average.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Where do you want this?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm not carrying anything. I'm just walking around with my hands out.

jokes.text: 'Chandler wants you to have a baby, but he doesn't want your body to change. It's not like he's so perfect.'
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel discuss Chandler's apparent anxiety about Monica's body changing with pregnancy.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's defense of Monica involves noting that Chandler is not himself 'so perfect' — a barely qualified insult of Chandler's physique.
jokes.explanation: Generic appearance-based put-down of Chandler without character specificity or a fresh angle. 'Not so perfect' is vague and punches in the least interesting direction. Monica's 'Hey, that's my husband' response rescues the beat slightly but the joke itself is thin. Among the weaker comedy beats in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What? What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I just realized... you want to get married.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Aahhhhh!

jokes.text: Ross enters and compliments Rachel: 'Hey, Rach. Perfection. Wouldn't change a thing. Not a thing.'
jokes.setup: Ross continues his campaign to prevent Rachel from getting a boob job
jokes.punchline: His compliments have become so mechanical that 'perfection' and 'not a thing' are delivered like a nervous mantra
jokes.explanation: Functional repeat of the earlier joke. The diminishing returns of Ross's campaign are the joke, but this iteration doesn't add much. Gets a small laugh from recognition.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know this is a big moment, but we really need to figure out the logistics here. Where are we putting the couch?

jokes.text: Rachel explains she's going to get bigger — referring to pregnancy. Ross says 'I love your breasts the way they are.' Rachel: 'Fascist.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is talking about her body changing during pregnancy; Ross thinks she's talking about a boob job
jokes.punchline: Ross's declaration of love for her breasts as-is — meant to prevent surgery — is received as body fascism by Rachel, who is talking about pregnancy
jokes.explanation: 'Fascist' as a one-word comeback to 'I love your breasts the way they are' is excellent economy. The cross-purpose misunderstanding structure has built to a genuinely funny confrontation and 'Fascist' is the right level of Rachel dramatic escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh Phoebe, I'm so sorry about you and Frank Jr. But hey, look on the bright side - now you can finally redecorate that apartment! I've been dying to get in there with some throw pillows and a nice area rug.

jokes.text: 'Fascist.'
jokes.setup: Chandler says 'I love your breasts the way they are' — apparently in response to what he thinks is Monica planning to enlarge them.
jokes.punchline: Monica interprets his love of her current breasts as a form of oppression — calling him a 'fascist' for supposedly mandating their size.
jokes.explanation: One word. 'Fascist' as a response to 'I love your breasts the way they are' is a spectacular single-word punchline. The political escalation is absurd and perfectly Monica — she's not joking, she genuinely finds his breast opinion to be authoritarian overreach. The word is so disproportionately large for the situation that it becomes perfect. Maximum economy (10/10 — one word conveys everything). The rewatch bonus comes from the layers: Monica thinks he's policing her pregnant body, Chandler thinks she's planning cosmetic surgery — the word 'Fascist' perfectly encapsulates the misunderstanding's absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: His furniture is so ugly. I can't believe I dated him.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Um, Monica? You're still dating him.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'And it's not just my breasts. My ass is gonna get bigger too.' / Ross: 'Your ass?!'
jokes.setup: Rachel continues listing her pregnancy body changes; Ross continues to hear this as boob-job-related surgery plans
jokes.punchline: Ross's horror at 'your ass?!' — a man who thought he was dealing with one surgery now confronted with what he thinks is comprehensive body modification
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke. Ross's escalating horror as Rachel keeps adding body parts to the list is a solid misunderstanding payoff. 'Your ass?!' is delivered with the energy of a man having a breakdown, which is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey Phoebe, I'm really sorry about you and Mike. That's rough.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Thanks Joey. I just... I can't believe it's over.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's terrible. Hey, Mike's got any of that good leftover pasta in here?

jokes.text: Monica: 'And don't be surprised if her hands and her feet get bigger too.' / Ross: 'They do that?' / Monica: 'It's kind of a package deal.'
jokes.setup: Monica adds to Rachel's list of pregnancy body changes — this time, the extremities
jokes.punchline: Ross's 'They do that?' — genuine horrified ignorance about basic pregnancy facts — is the joke, capped by Monica's flat 'It's kind of a package deal'
jokes.explanation: Good beat. 'It's kind of a package deal' as Monica's exasperated summary of pregnancy is well-delivered. Ross's ignorance of basic biology despite being a scientist and already having a child from his first marriage is an extra layer of irony.

jokes.text: Ross: 'God, why? Why would you want to do that to yourself?'
jokes.setup: Ross still thinks Rachel is choosing elective surgery
jokes.punchline: His anguished 'why would you want to do that to yourself?' about pregnancy — the most natural thing — reveals his complete confusion
jokes.explanation: Functional misunderstanding joke. The irony of Ross — a paleontologist — being baffled that a pregnant woman's body would change is a mild laugh but not a strong joke on its own. Setup for the bigger reveal.

jokes.text: Ross: 'I may be able to get onboard with the boobs, but the giant ass and the big clown feet?'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to negotiate with what he thinks is Rachel's surgery plan
jokes.punchline: 'Big clown feet' as his term for pregnancy-enlarged feet — delivered in horrified sincerity — is both funny and character-revealing in its obliviousness
jokes.explanation: 'Big clown feet' is the right phrase — specific, cruel, and unintentionally so. Ross is horrified by what he thinks is an elective choice while actually describing pregnancy. The escalation of 'giant ass' to 'big clown feet' is a good comedic list.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Oh my God, Chandler. If you can't handle this, what will you be like in the hospital with the blood and the screaming and the little person that's shooting out of her?'
jokes.setup: Chandler is freaking out about pregnancy body changes
jokes.punchline: 'The little person that's shooting out of her' — Monica's clinical-casual description of childbirth — is both blunt and funny
jokes.explanation: 'Shooting out of her' is a great absurdist-realist description of birth. Monica's matter-of-fact delivery of something horrifying is character-appropriate and sets up Chandler's breakdown.

jokes.text: Chandler's reaction: 'What?!' [after learning Rachel isn't getting a boob job — she's just pregnant and her body will change naturally]
jokes.setup: The whole misunderstanding about Rachel's 'boob job' has been building — Chandler now realizes she's not planning surgery at all
jokes.punchline: Chandler's simple 'What?!' — the collision of the two misunderstandings (he thought Monica wanted surgery; Monica and Rachel thought Ross thought Rachel wanted surgery; actually Rachel is just pregnant) all landing at once
jokes.explanation: Effective reaction beat payoff to the episode's main farce plot. The 'What?!' lands hard because of the accumulated confusion. Good economy — one word to unravel the whole plot.

jokes.text: Chandler hears that Monica is talking about pregnancy, not a boob job: 'What?'
jokes.setup: Joey reveals to Chandler (and us) that Monica is talking about pregnancy changes, while Chandler has been panicking about a boob job.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's dawning realization — 'What?' — that the entire scene has been about pregnancy and he's been objecting to his wife getting pregnant.
jokes.explanation: The reveal beat that closes the boob job plotline. Chandler's single 'What?' carries the weight of the entire misunderstanding collapsing at once — he now realizes he's been opposing his own desired pregnancy. Good reaction beat. The rewatch bonus is high because on rewatch, every earlier awkward exchange is recontextualized.

jokes.text: Monica confronts Joey: 'Joey, why did you tell Chandler that Monica was getting a boob job?' / Joey: 'Because she is.' / Monica: 'Chandler knows I borrowed the money.' / Joey: 'For your boob job.' / Monica: '...Joe.' / Joey: 'It's over.'
jokes.setup: Monica confronts Joey about his error
jokes.punchline: Joey's stubborn insistence — 'It's over' — when confronted with the truth, as if the boob job is an established fact he refuses to un-know
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the episode's central misunderstanding. 'It's over' — said with resignation rather than apology — is the right Joey response. He's not correcting himself; he's mourning the boob job. Character-perfect.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Okay, so I'm out $4000 and nobody's boobs are getting any bigger?'
jokes.setup: The whole misunderstanding is resolved — no boob jobs happened, Joey is out $4000
jokes.punchline: Joey's summary of the situation focuses entirely on the boob-job angle and his financial loss — his priorities crystallized in one sentence
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a strong candidate for its single best line. Joey reduces the entire emotional misunderstanding to two things: money and breasts. The specificity of '$4000' (combining both loans) shows he's been doing math, but his conclusion — 'nobody's boobs are getting any bigger?' — reveals his actual concern. It's character-perfect, quotable, and lands as the episode's comedic thesis. The outrage is completely sincere from Joey's perspective, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Hey, you guys, what do you think about this: Ross, the Divorce Force.'
jokes.setup: Earlier Ross tried 'Ross, the Divorcer' and was told it wasn't cool
jokes.punchline: He's iterated to 'Ross, the Divorce Force' — which is actually slightly better but still absurd
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. The fact that Ross has been workshopping his divorce rebrand — arriving at 'Divorce Force,' which rhymes and has even more superhero energy — is a great character beat. The group's approval ('Better. Yeah, very cool.') while still being ridiculous is the right ending for the running gag. Ross's earnest investment in his own branding is a core character truth.

jokes.text: Ross to Phoebe, unsolicited: 'I don't think marriage is necessarily the right path for you... can you honestly picture yourself in a Volvo? They are awfully boxy.'
jokes.setup: Ross is now trying to talk Phoebe out of wanting marriage after learning she does want it
jokes.punchline: He undermines Phoebe's soccer-mom fantasy by going back to the Volvo — which Phoebe immediately agrees is 'awfully boxy' — the most trivial possible reason to abandon a life goal
jokes.explanation: Good callback that uses the earlier Volvo joke as a pivot point for Ross's manipulation. Phoebe's immediate agreement ('they are awfully boxy') is funny — she's being talked out of marriage by car aesthetics. Character-appropriate for both.

jokes.text: Mike (struggling to carry furniture up stairs): 'Well, we climbed up four flights of stairs, maneuvered a narrow hallway, dodged a rabid pit bull. But these last three feet are where it gets really tricky.'
jokes.setup: Mike and movers are struggling to bring furniture into Phoebe's apartment
jokes.punchline: Mike's dry catalogue of obstacles — culminating in 'rabid pit bull' — delivered as a matter-of-fact logistical summary is the joke, with 'but these last three feet' as the understatement payoff
jokes.explanation: Decent physical comedy with a good list structure. The 'rabid pit bull' detail is funny in its inclusion alongside mundane obstacles. 'But these last three feet are where it gets really tricky' is well-delivered understatement.

jokes.text: 'Well, we climbed up four flights of stairs, maneuvered a narrow hallway, dodged a rabid pit bull. But these last three feet are where it gets really tricky.'
jokes.setup: Joey (or someone) asks if they need help moving a large piece of furniture. Mike explains the journey to get it this far.
jokes.punchline: The list of genuine obstacles — four flights of stairs, narrow hallway, actual rabid pit bull — builds an epic narrative, only to end with 'the last three feet are where it gets tricky' — the most modest possible conclusion.
jokes.explanation: The escalating catalog of obstacles topped by the self-deprecating reversal ('these last three feet') is a good structural beat. The rabid pit bull in the middle of the list is the highlight — delivered as a matter-of-fact obstacle alongside 'narrow hallway.' The understatement of 'really tricky' after surviving a pit bull is good comedy.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'You know, sometimes your words, they hurt.'
jokes.setup: Mike has implicitly criticized Phoebe's neighborhood (rabid pit bulls, narrow hallways)
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's dignified complaint — 'sometimes your words, they hurt' — in the middle of a physical comedy scene is a funny contrast
jokes.explanation: Light laugh. The injured dignity of 'sometimes your words, they hurt' is a standard sitcom beat but Phoebe's delivery makes it work.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, seriously, because this is really heavy. I mean, not for me, because I'm only pretending to hold it, but for these guys.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is helping move a heavy piece of furniture.
jokes.punchline: Joey admits he is 'only pretending to hold it' — not helping at all, while positioning himself as an advocate for those doing the actual work.
jokes.explanation: Joey publicly confessing to pretending to hold a heavy item — without shame, while advocating for others — is perfectly Joey. The structure of the admission is good: 'really heavy, not for me, because I'm only pretending' — the reason clause makes the joke. High character integration: Joey's self-serving laziness combined with his pseudo-solidarity is exactly his character.

jokes.text: Joey (pretending to hold furniture): 'Yeah, seriously, because this is really heavy. I mean, not for me, because I'm only pretending to hold it, but for these guys.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is helping move furniture
jokes.punchline: Joey cheerfully admits he's not actually helping while expressing sympathy for the people who are
jokes.explanation: Good Joey joke. His completely open admission that he's faking physical effort — combined with genuine concern for others — is a perfect character beat. The logic ('not for me, because I'm only pretending') is classic Joey oblivious self-interest wrapped in apparent sympathy. The transition to 'but for these guys' as if that makes it okay is excellent.

jokes.text: Mike: 'Couldn't have had this conversation down at the truck, huh?'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just revealed (while on the fourth floor, in the middle of moving) that she actually does want to get married someday
jokes.punchline: Mike's comment is entirely practical — why are we having this life-changing conversation while holding furniture on the fourth floor?
jokes.explanation: Good dry joke. The domestic comedy of this enormous emotional conversation happening at the worst possible physical moment is funny. Mike's perfectly flat 'Couldn't have had this conversation down at the truck, huh?' is the right deflection. Good economy.

jokes.text: Mike: 'And... hernia.'
jokes.setup: Mike is struggling to hold the furniture while having an emotionally devastating conversation with Phoebe
jokes.punchline: 'And... hernia.' — delivered flatly as if the physical injury is just one more thing on the list of this terrible moment
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy joke. Two words — 'And... hernia.' — do enormous work: they acknowledge the physical pain, undercut the emotional moment, and Mike's complete composure despite the injury is funny. The pause before 'hernia' is crucial (implied by the ellipsis). Perfect physical/deadpan combination. High quotability.

jokes.text: Mike (carrying furniture, finding out Phoebe wants marriage): 'I said to bring the cushions up first, but no.'
jokes.setup: The relationship-ending conversation about marriage is happening while furniture is being hauled up stairs
jokes.punchline: Mike's aside — blaming the logistics of the furniture move rather than engaging with the emotional content — is a perfect deadpan deflection
jokes.explanation: Very good deadpan. 'I said to bring the cushions up first, but no' — blaming the furniture logistics for the emotional chaos — is Mike's character in one line. It's the British stiff-upper-lip response to romantic catastrophe. The 'but no' as an exhausted coda is perfect.

jokes.text: Joey, after Phoebe and Mike's breakup: 'Look on the bright side. At least you won't have to live with this ugly chair.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is comforting Phoebe after her heartbreaking split from Mike
jokes.punchline: Joey's attempt at comfort focuses on the furniture — specifically criticizing the chair as ugly — which is both oblivious to the situation and a genuinely Joey way to make someone feel better
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character jokes. Joey's attempt at consolation — focused on a material object rather than the emotional devastation — is perfectly in character. 'At least you won't have to live with this ugly chair' as a silver lining for a heartbreak is both obtuse and oddly sweet. The line is completely Joey-specific. Monica's reality check ('That was here already, huh?') is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Joey, looking at the abandoned furniture: 'I'd better take all I can carry. Who knows when I'll be able to get in here again, huh?'
jokes.setup: The emotionally devastating breakup has left Phoebe's apartment full of Mike's furniture
jokes.punchline: Joey's takeaway from his friend's heartbreak is an opportunity to loot the abandoned furniture
jokes.explanation: Excellent episode-closing Joey joke. His pivot from friend support to opportunistic furniture looting — framed as prudent rather than predatory ('who knows when I'll be able to get in here again') — is perfectly in character. The tone of 'I'd better take all I can carry' implies this is a reasonable response to any situation. Character-perfect and funny as a tag.

jokes.text: Joey raiding Monica and Chandler's fridge at the end: 'I'd better take all I can carry. Who knows when I'll be able to get in here again, huh?'
jokes.setup: Everyone has had an emotional and chaotic episode. Joey takes the opportunity of the unlocked apartment.
jokes.punchline: Joey treats Monica's fridge as a natural resource to be harvested — 'I'd better take all I can carry' — and treats his regular access as potentially under threat, even though it's not.
jokes.explanation: A good closing character beat for Joey — the episode ends on him doing what Joey always does: thinking about food. 'Who knows when I'll be able to get in here again' implies some ongoing territorial anxiety about fridge access that is entirely in Joey's head. Good character button for the episode.

tmdb_overview: While reviewing their monthly expenses, Monica and Chandler discover that their situation is less than stellar. This results in Monica asking Joey to lend her some money without telling Chandler. When Chandler eventually finds out, Joey comes up with a lie that Monica needs the money for breast enhancement procedure. Meanwhile, Phoebe gets really excited as she and Mike decide to move in together, but her excitement quickly dissipates once she discovers that Mike doesn't see himself getting married ever again. Also, Rachel's attempt to baby-proof the apartment tampers with a frustrated Joey's sanity.
insight: Phoebe's body-swap obsession anchors 69 jokes at middling 70.4 impact.
